t: Widest Pair of Indices With Equal Range Sum - Prefix Difference Hashing
o: We need the widest window [i..j] where nums1 and nums2 have equal element sums. Subtract prefix sums: with D(k) defined as (sum of nums1[0..k]) minus (sum of nums2[0..k]), window equality collapses to D(j) == D(i-1). So the task becomes finding two equal values of D as far apart as possible over prefix positions -1 through n-1, with D(-1) = 0. In Example 1 the running differences after each index are 1, 1, 0, 1; value 0 appears at virtual position -1 and again at index 2, so window [0..2] has equal sums 2 and 2, distance 3. Example 2 repeats -1 exactly one step apart, answering 1, and Example 3 never repeats any value, answering 0. With n up to 100000, checking all windows in quadratic time is off the table.
k: Equal range sums of nums1 and nums2 over [i..j] are equivalent to their prefix-sum difference taking the same value at positions j and i-1.
The longest span between equal values is found by remembering only the FIRST index at which each difference value occurs.
Seeding the map with value 0 at index -1 covers windows that start at index 0.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Windows
a.i: Fix each start index i and extend the window one step at a time, maintaining both running sums incrementally so each (i, j) pair costs O(1). Whenever the sums agree, update the best width. This directly mirrors the definition and is a useful correctness reference, but it touches every pair of endpoints.
s: For each start i, initialize both running sums to 0.
Extend j from i to n-1, adding nums1[j] and nums2[j] to their respective sums.
If the sums are equal, update best with j - i + 1.
Return best after all starts are tried.
a.t: O(n^2) - every start index scans to the end of both arrays, which times out at n = 10^5
a.sp: O(1) - only two running sums besides the answer

a.n: Approach 2: First Occurrence of Each Prefix Difference
a.i: Sweep left to right maintaining D = prefix1 - prefix2. If D was seen before at position p (seeded with 0 at -1), the window [p+1..i] has equal sums, contributing width i - p; otherwise record this as the first occurrence of D. Because we only ever store first occurrences, every later repeat measures the widest possible span for that value, so one linear pass is optimal.
s: Initialize map first with {0: -1} and running difference d = 0.
For each index i, update d by adding nums1[i] - nums2[i].
If d is already in the map, update the answer with i - first[d].
Otherwise insert first[d] = i (keep only the earliest occurrence).
Return the maximum width found, or 0.
a.t: O(n) - one pass with expected O(1) hash operations per index
a.sp: O(n) - the map stores at most n+1 distinct difference values

w: Go straight to the prefix-difference hash in an interview; the brute force serves only as a warm-up and validator. Pitfalls: forgetting the seed entry 0 at index -1 (windows starting at index 0 then vanish), and mishandling the geometry of a repeated value seen at prefix positions p and i: it corresponds to window [p+1..i], whose length is exactly i - p. Storing later occurrences instead of the earliest would shrink every measured span. Follow-ups: widest window whose sums differ by at most k, or counting all equal-sum windows.
